Some invocations occasionally fail with ProvisionedThroughputExceededException from DynamoDB during traffic bursts, and the function has no dead-letter destination configured, so failed asynchronous invocations are simply retried by Lambda and then silently discarded after exhausting retries. The team needs visibility into permanently failed events and a way to reprocess them later. What should the developer configure?
options: Configure an on-failure destination, such as an SQS queue, on the Lambda function's asynchronous invocation configuration
Add a try/catch block in the function that logs the error to CloudWatch Logs
Enable DynamoDB auto scaling on the write capacity only
Increase the function's reserved concurrency to prevent throttling
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because destinations capture the final failed event payload after Lambda's automatic retries are exhausted, so it can be inspected and reprocessed instead of being discarded silently. Option B is incorrect because logging captures information about the failure but does not preserve the event for automated reprocessing the way a destination does. Option C is incorrect because auto scaling can help reduce throttling over time but does not provide visibility into or recovery of already-failed events. Option D is incorrect because this may reduce concurrent execution contention but does nothing to capture or preserve events that ultimately fail. On-failure destinations (or a DLQ) are the mechanism for capturing permanently failed asynchronous Lambda invocations for later handling.

questions.question: A team observes that requests to a REST API on API Gateway backed by Lambda intermittently take over 3 seconds, while most requests complete in under 200 ms. X-Ray is enabled on both API Gateway and the Lambda function. Which X-Ray capability should the team use first to pinpoint where the extra latency occurs in the slow requests?
options: Enable X-Ray on the underlying EC2 instances hosting API Gateway
Examine the trace timeline (segments and subsegments) for a sample of the slow requests to see which segment, such as Lambda initialization or a downstream call, accounts for the added time
Increase the X-Ray sampling rate to capture 100% of requests
Add more X-Ray annotations to the Lambda function's code
questions.explanation: Option A is incorrect because API Gateway and Lambda are managed services without customer-visible EC2 instances to instrument in this way. Option B is correct because the trace timeline breaks a single request down into its constituent segments and subsegments with timing, directly showing which part of the request is slow. Option C is incorrect because a higher sampling rate captures more traces for analysis, but the team already has traces for the slow requests and needs to inspect their breakdown, not to just capture more. Option D is incorrect because annotations make traces searchable by custom key-value pairs; they do not by themselves reveal which segment of an already-captured trace is slow. The trace timeline view is the direct tool for seeing which part of a specific request's execution consumed the most time.

questions.question: A DynamoDB table configured with on-demand capacity mode is experiencing ThrottlingException errors on a small number of specific item keys during a flash sale, while overall table-level consumed capacity remains well under the account's default limits. What is the most likely cause, and what should the developer do?
options: Requests are concentrated on a hot partition key, exceeding the per-partition throughput limit; the developer should redesign the key schema to distribute traffic, for example by adding a random suffix or sharding the key
On-demand tables have a hard limit of 40,000 read and 40,000 write units total, and the account has exceeded it
On-demand mode does not support bursts, so the table should be switched to provisioned mode with auto scaling
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) must be added in front of the table to handle any burst of traffic
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because even in on-demand mode, DynamoDB enforces a per-partition throughput limit, so traffic concentrated on very few partition key values can be throttled while the table's aggregate capacity looks fine. Option B is incorrect because the scenario states overall consumed capacity is well under limits, and the described throttling pattern targeting specific keys points to a partition-level hot key issue, not an account-wide ceiling. Option C is incorrect because provisioned mode does not remove per-partition limits either; switching modes would not resolve a hot-key distribution problem. Option D is incorrect because DAX helps with read-heavy caching workloads but does not fix write throttling caused by a skewed partition key. Hot partition keys can throttle specific requests even when table-wide capacity metrics look healthy; the fix is better key distribution, not simply adding capacity.

questions.question: A developer is debugging a Lambda function and wants to understand the fastest ways to test its behavior against specific inputs. Which TWO approaches let the developer test the function directly with a chosen JSON payload without waiting for a real event source to trigger it? (Select TWO)
options: Enable enhanced monitoring on the function's log group
Call the Lambda Invoke API (or aws lambda invoke in the CLI) with a JSON payload file
Wait for a production request that happens to match the desired input
Use the Lambda console's Test feature with a saved test event
Modify the function code to hardcode the input temporarily and redeploy
questions.explanation: Option A is incorrect because enhanced monitoring only affects what metrics or logs are captured; it does not invoke the function with a chosen input. Option B is correct because the Invoke API lets a caller send an arbitrary payload directly to the function outside of any event source integration. Option C is incorrect because this is unreliable and slow compared to directly invoking the function with a chosen payload. Option D is correct because the console's Test feature invokes the function synchronously with whatever payload is saved as the test event and immediately shows the response and logs. Option E is incorrect because this requires an unnecessary code change and deployment cycle just to test one input. Direct invocation, either through the console test feature or the Invoke API/CLI, is the fastest way to exercise a Lambda function with a specific payload.

questions.question: An Application Load Balancer's target group reports that newly registered EC2 targets stay in the 'initial' state and then become 'unhealthy', even though the application logs show it started successfully and is listening on the configured port. The security group attached to the instances allows inbound traffic only from the application's own client IP range on the application port. What is the most likely fix?
options: Enable cross-zone load balancing on the load balancer
Switch the target group's target type from instance to IP
Update the instance security group to allow inbound traffic from the load balancer (for example, its security group) on the health check port and path
Increase the health check timeout value only
questions.explanation: Option A is incorrect because cross-zone load balancing controls how traffic is distributed across zones and does not affect whether health checks can reach a target. Option B is incorrect because the target type affects how targets are registered, not whether the security group permits the load balancer's health check traffic. Option C is correct because the load balancer's health checks originate from its own network interfaces, so the target's security group must allow traffic from the load balancer, not just from end-user client IPs. Option D is incorrect because adjusting timing settings does not address a security group that is blocking the health check traffic entirely. Targets must allow inbound traffic from the load balancer for health checks to succeed; restricting to only end-user IPs blocks the load balancer itself.

questions.question: A team notices that CloudWatch billing shows a much higher-than-expected Lambda invocation count for a function subscribed to an SNS topic, roughly matching the number of SNS publish retries during a recent outage of the function's downstream dependency, which caused the function to throw exceptions. The team wants to reduce redundant invocations while still eventually processing every message. What should they configure?
options: Switch the SNS topic to a FIFO topic to eliminate duplicate deliveries
Disable retries entirely on the SNS subscription
Add a dead-letter queue (or on-failure destination) to the SNS subscription and reduce unnecessary duplicate processing by making the function idempotent so repeated deliveries are handled safely
Reduce the Lambda function's memory allocation to lower cost per invocation
questions.explanation: Option A is incorrect because FIFO topics provide deduplication for messages published within their deduplication interval, but they do not eliminate SNS's normal retry behavior toward a failing subscriber, and switching topic types is a significant architecture change unrelated to the root cause. Option B is incorrect because disabling retries would cause messages to be dropped whenever the function fails, which fails the requirement to eventually process every message. Option C is correct because SNS retries deliveries to a failing subscriber, and idempotent handling combined with a DLQ ensures that repeated or ultimately failed deliveries are handled safely and captured instead of silently reprocessed forever. Option D is incorrect because lowering memory does not reduce the number of invocations caused by retries; it may even slow down processing. Handling downstream failures safely requires idempotency plus a DLQ/destination for messages that cannot be delivered, not disabling retries.

questions.question: A serverless application's Lambda function reads a large reference dataset from S3 on every cold start, adding around 4 seconds to cold start latency. The dataset changes only once a day. The team wants to reduce this latency for cold starts without moving to a different compute service. Which optimization is most effective?
options: Reduce the memory allocated to the function to lower cost
Use Lambda SnapStart (for supported runtimes) or cache the dataset in /tmp with a check for freshness, loading it once per execution environment instead of downloading it on every cold start
Increase the function's timeout to allow the download to complete
Move the dataset download into the function handler so it happens on every invocation
questions.explanation: Option A is incorrect because lower memory generally reduces available CPU and network throughput, which would make the download slower, not faster. Option B is correct because SnapStart resumes from a pre-initialized, cached snapshot after initialization has already run once, and caching the dataset locally across warm invocations avoids repeating the download for the lifetime of that execution environment. Option C is incorrect because a longer timeout only allows the slow operation to finish; it does not make the operation faster or avoid repeating it. Option D is incorrect because moving initialization work into the handler makes even warm invocations pay the cost repeatedly, which is worse, not better. Cold start optimizations focus on doing expensive initialization once per execution environment (or using SnapStart) rather than on every invocation.

questions.question: A developer wants to know exactly how much time a specific Lambda function invocation spent in the initialization phase versus execution, to help decide whether provisioned concurrency would help. Where can the developer find this breakdown for a specific invocation?
options: The REPORT line in the function's CloudWatch Logs, which includes Init Duration for cold starts along with Duration and Billed Duration
The Lambda function's configured memory size shown in the console
The function's reserved concurrency setting
The IAM execution role's last-used timestamp
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because Lambda automatically logs a REPORT line after each invocation, and cold starts include an Init Duration field showing initialization time separately from execution duration. Option B is incorrect because the configured memory is a static setting and does not show per-invocation timing information. Option C is incorrect because reserved concurrency is a capacity control and provides no timing breakdown of an invocation. Option D is incorrect because the role's last-used timestamp only shows when the role was last used for any action, not invocation timing details. The REPORT log line, especially its Init Duration field on cold starts, is the direct source for per-invocation timing breakdowns.

questions.question: A Lambda function that processes messages from a standard SQS queue is scaling up but the queue's ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric keeps growing, indicating the consumer is falling behind. The function's concurrent executions are far below the account's concurrency limit and below the function's own reserved concurrency. What is the most likely explanation?
options: DynamoDB Streams must be enabled for SQS-triggered functions to scale properly
The function's timeout is set too high, which is preventing Lambda from scaling
The SQS event source mapping's maximum concurrency (or the number of pollers based on queue and Lambda scaling) is limiting how quickly Lambda scales up to consume the backlog
SQS standard queues have a hard limit of 10 in-flight messages per consumer
questions.explanation: Option A is incorrect because DynamoDB Streams are unrelated to how Lambda scales against an SQS-triggered event source mapping. Option B is incorrect because a high timeout by itself does not prevent Lambda from adding more concurrent executions to drain a queue backlog. Option C is correct because Lambda's SQS event source mapping scales gradually and can also be capped by a configured maximum concurrency setting on the mapping itself, independent of the function's reserved concurrency or account-wide limits. Option D is incorrect because standard queues support a very large number of in-flight messages (up to 120,000 depending on configuration), not a limit of 10. Event source mapping scaling behavior and any explicit MaximumConcurrency setting can bottleneck SQS-to-Lambda throughput independent of account or reserved concurrency limits.

questions.question: A developer needs to correlate a slow customer-reported request across API Gateway, a Lambda function, and a downstream HTTP call to a third-party service, using a single trace ID passed through all layers. Which AWS capability directly supports this correlated, end-to-end view?
options: AWS X-Ray tracing enabled on API Gateway and Lambda, with the X-Ray SDK instrumenting the downstream HTTP call
AWS Config aggregated resource history
Amazon CloudWatch composite alarms
CloudWatch Logs Insights across each service's separate log group
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because X-Ray propagates a trace ID across service boundaries and stitches segments from each instrumented component into a single, correlated trace. Option B is incorrect because Config tracks configuration changes over time for resources, not the execution path of a specific application request. Option C is incorrect because composite alarms combine the state of several alarms into one; they do not provide request-level tracing. Option D is incorrect because Logs Insights can query multiple log groups, but without a shared trace ID it cannot automatically correlate related log lines from different services into one request view. X-Ray is the AWS service purpose-built to correlate a single request's path across multiple integrated services using a shared trace ID.
